article.headline: Cuban gold tarantula care guide
article.description: A detailed guide to keeping Phormictopus auratus: size, terrarium, substrate, temperature, humidity, feeding, hairs and moulting.

name: Cuban gold tarantula
lead: A large tarantula from Cuba with a dark body and a golden-bronze sheen. Fast, voracious and impressive - for keepers who already have some experience.
photoAlt: Cuban gold tarantula (Phormictopus auratus) - NS Reptiles Novi Sad
intro: The Cuban gold tarantula (Phormictopus auratus) is a large terrestrial tarantula from Cuba. After a moult its dark body shows a strong golden-bronze sheen. It grows fast and almost never refuses food, but it is nervous and often defensive, so it makes a better second or third tarantula than a first one. To get started, we also offer a tarantula starter kit with an enclosure and substrate.

boxes.title: Origin and habitat
p: It comes from Cuba, where it lives on the ground in drier forests and scrubland, in burrows it digs itself or takes over.

boxes.title: Size and appearance
p: A large tarantula: adult females reach a leg span of about 15 cm, some even more. The body is dark, and after a moult the hairs have a golden-bronze sheen that gives the species its name.

boxes.title: Behaviour
p: Fast and nervous - when disturbed it takes a threat posture with raised front legs and is ready to bite. It is extremely voracious and attacks prey immediately. Its temperament makes it unsuitable for beginners, but it is great to watch.

boxes.title: Terrarium
p: This is a terrestrial species, so it needs a horizontal terrarium - floor space matters more than height. An adult needs an enclosure with a floor of about 40×30 cm. Leave only a few centimetres more than the spider's leg span above the substrate: a fall can rupture the abdomen and be fatal. The lid must close tightly, and ventilation should be both on the sides and on top. Spiderlings are kept in smaller containers, in proportion to their size.

boxes.title: Substrate
p: Provide 10–15 cm of substrate, as it likes to dig: coco peat or a mix of peat and fertiliser-free soil. The lower layer should be moderately moist and the surface drier.

boxes.title: Hide and decor
p: A half cork bark or a piece of bark as a hide, a shallow water dish and a few dry leaves or artificial plants are enough. Place heavier items on the bottom before adding substrate, so they cannot fall on the spider while it digs. Do not overcrowd the enclosure.

boxes.title: Temperature and light
p: Room temperature of about 22–27 °C suits it. If it gets colder in winter, put a heat mat on a side or back wall, never under the substrate - the spider escapes heat by digging down, so heating from below could overheat it. No special lighting or UVB is needed; avoid direct sunlight.

boxes.title: Humidity and water
p: Humidity of about 60–70% suits it. Moisten the substrate from time to time by watering one corner. A shallow dish of clean water should always be in the enclosure.

boxes.title: Prey
p: It feeds on live insects: crickets, roaches (e.g. dubia), locusts and similar prey. Prey should not be larger than the spider's abdomen. Do not feed wild-caught insects, as they may carry parasites and pesticides.

boxes.title: Feeding frequency
p: Adults need food once a week or less, spiderlings twice a week with smaller prey. Remove prey that is not eaten within a day. It is normal for a tarantula to refuse food for weeks before a moult - do not offer food then.

boxes.title: Urticating hairs
p: Like other tarantulas from the Americas, it has urticating hairs on the abdomen that it flicks off with its legs when threatened. On the skin they cause itching and redness, and in the eyes serious irritation. Keep your face away when working in the enclosure and wash your hands afterwards. When disturbed, it defends itself more often with a threat posture and a bite than with hairs.

boxes.title: Venom
p: The venom of this species is not dangerous to a healthy person - a bite is comparable to a bee or wasp sting: pain, redness and swelling that pass. As with a bee sting, an allergic reaction is possible; if breathing becomes difficult or swelling spreads, seek medical help immediately.

boxes.title: Handling
p: We do not recommend handling. A fall from just a few dozen centimetres can be fatal for a tarantula, and a frightened spider may bite or flick hairs. To move it, guide the spider into a clear container and cover it with a piece of card. Keep the enclosure out of reach of children and pets.

boxes.title: Growth and lifespan
p: It grows fast for a tarantula. Females live more than 10 years, males much less - usually a year or two after maturing.

boxes.title: Moulting
p: A tarantula grows by moulting. Before a moult it stops eating and its abdomen darkens. It usually moults lying on its back - this is normal and not a sign of death, so do not touch it. After the moult wait at least a week before feeding, until the new exoskeleton and fangs harden. No live prey may be left in the enclosure at that time.

boxes.title: Possible problems
p: The biggest risks are falls, dehydration and live prey left in during a moult. A spider pulling its legs under its body is a serious sign - check that it has water and contact an experienced breeder or an exotic animal vet. Mould and mites appear in an overly wet, poorly ventilated enclosure with food leftovers.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about the cuban gold tarantula

items.q: Is the cuban gold tarantula venomous?
items.a: It is not dangerous to a healthy person - a bite is similar to a bee sting. The bigger nuisance is the urticating hairs from the abdomen, which irritate the skin and eyes.

items.q: How big does the cuban gold tarantula get?
items.a: Adult females reach a leg span of about 15 cm, some even more.

items.q: How long does the cuban gold tarantula live?
items.a: Females more than 10 years, males much less.

items.q: What does the cuban gold tarantula eat?
items.a: Live insects of the right size - crickets, roaches and locusts. Adults only need feeding once a week or less.

items.q: Is the cuban gold tarantula good for beginners?
items.a: We do not recommend it as a first tarantula - it is fast, nervous and quick to defend itself. It is an excellent choice for someone who already has experience with calmer species.

items.q: Can you handle a cuban gold tarantula?
items.a: We do not recommend it. A fall can be fatal for the spider, and a frightened tarantula may bite or flick irritating hairs. Use a container to move it.
